questions.q: For a joint table with $p(x,y) = p(x)\,p(y)$ in every cell, what is $I(X;Y)$?
questions.explain: Then $H(X,Y) = H(X) + H(Y)$, so $I = H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y) = 0$; equivalently $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(x,y)\,\|\,p(x)p(y)) = 0$ because the two distributions are identical.

questions.q: $Y$ is an exact copy of $X$, where $X$ takes 3 values with probabilities $0.2, 0.3, 0.5$. What is $I(X;Y)$?
questions.explain: $H(Y\mid X) = 0$, so $I = H(Y) - 0 = H(X) \approx 1.485$ bits. $\log_2 3$ would only be reached if $X$ were uniform.

questions.q: A binary symmetric channel with uniform input flips each bit with probability $\varepsilon$. For which $\varepsilon$ is $I(X;Y) = 1 - H_b(\varepsilon)$ equal to 0?
questions.explain: $H_b(0.5) = 1$ bit, so $I = 0$: the output is a coin flip regardless of the input. At $\varepsilon = 1$ every bit is inverted — a perfectly predictable relation — so $I = 1 - H_b(1) = 1$ bit.

questions.q: With $x \sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1)$ and $y = x^2 + $ small noise, the page shows Pearson $r \approx 0$. What does the binned mutual information show, and why?
options: MI ≈ 0 too, because MI and correlation always agree
MI is clearly positive: knowing x pins down y, but the dependence is non-linear and symmetric so correlation cancels out
MI is negative, because the relationship slopes down for x < 0
MI is exactly 1 bit for any noise level and bin count
questions.explain: Correlation only measures linear dependence; the down-slope for $x<0$ cancels the up-slope for $x>0$. MI captures any dependence and is never negative. Its binned estimate depends on n and the bin count and is biased upward (compare the shuffled baseline).
